title: Balanced Brackets With std::stack
statement:
`(`, `[` and `{` each need to be closed by the matching `)`, `]` or `}` --
and closed in the right order: `([)]` is not balanced even though it has
one of each character, because the `[` opens *after* the `(` but closes
*before* it does. `std::stack<char>` is built for exactly this shape of
problem: the most recently opened bracket is always the first one that has
to close.

## Your function

```
bool IsBalanced(const std::string& text);
```

`text` may contain any characters; only `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}`
participate in the check, and every other character is ignored. Return
`true` if every closing bracket matches the type of the most recently
unclosed opening bracket, and no opening bracket is left unclosed at the
end.

## Watch out

- **`std::stack<char>::pop()` returns `void`.** Unlike some other
  languages' stack types, popping and reading the top element are two
  separate calls here: `text.top()` reads the value without removing it,
  `text.pop()` removes it without telling you what it was. To "pop and
  compare", read `.top()` first, then call `.pop()` -- calling `.pop()`
  and expecting it to hand the value back will not compile.
- **`.top()` and `.pop()` on an empty stack are undefined behaviour** --
  they do not throw, and do not fail loudly. A closing bracket that
  arrives with nothing open to match it (`text` starts with `)`, say) has
  to be checked for with `.empty()` *before* either call, not discovered
  by calling them anyway and hoping for a crash you can react to.
- **A stack that is not empty at the end means something was opened and
  never closed.** `"(()"` never sees a closing bracket it disagrees with
  -- every `)` it does see matches correctly -- so the mismatch can only
  be caught by checking the stack is empty once `text` is exhausted, not
  by anything that happens while consuming it.
